segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Ukraine, the government has set up this phone line. It's for soldiers to call-- Russian soldiers-- if they want to surrender.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [CONNECTING TONE]

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ukraine's says over 3,500 soldiers have texted or called the number. One of my coworkers, Valerie Kipnis, has been looking into this hotline, and helpfully, speaks Russian. So what did they just say?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So they said, hello, to one another, and then the guy asked, is this Ukraine? And the guy on the hotline answered, yeah, this is Ukraine.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And then, the soldier said, I got a text that if we wish to surrender, call this number.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He got a text?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah, people pass around the number on social media and Telegram. There's even a website for it. It's called Hochy-Zhit dot com.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And that means--

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: "I want to live" dot com.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's very direct.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. On it, it reads, "Servicemen of the Russian armed forces, do you notice that you're greeted not with flowers, but with fire and curses? Do you notice that your commanders run away first? Save your life, for yourself and your family. Stop fighting for other people's slogans. Contact us. Save your life."

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so what happens in this call?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: One interesting thing is that the guy doesn't seem to know if he can actually believe them. He's questioning if he can trust them.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He's saying, you won't be cutting our balls off?

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And then, the hotline guy answers, no, those are myths you guys are being fed. No one's going to be cutting anybody.

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Don't worry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, but can I ask you, like, why would somebody who's calling this number-- like, why would they trust them?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Well, obviously, it's a scary decision, and they have to judge it for themselves. But on the website, it says, you know, we follow the Geneva Conventions for the treatment of prisoners of war. And they say they guarantee certain things-- three meals a day, medical service, legal support from international organizations, and regular communication with relatives.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What else happens in this call?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Well, there's a bunch of stuff about, how does this actually work? Like, how do I surrender?

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Where should we come by? The soldier asks.

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The hotline guy says, if you're fighting, then you're probably located in a certain region.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Well, yeah. And you'll come pick us up?

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. We need to understand where you are and whether you really want to surrender. For that, I need your information, and then I'll contact you.

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And then, you can surrender, if you wish.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Does the soldier sound nervous to you?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. On the call, you can kind of hear him trying to make the decision of whether to do this or not.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: We didn't even want to come here. We were ordered. Now, I'm thinking about what I can do. The guy in the hotline says, so, as I'm telling you, if you want to, you can surrender, and then return back home.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Please understand there's a Geneva convention that says that a combatant has no criminal liability, so long as he did not commit war crimes, in which case, you'll be returned home through a prisoner swap.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The soldier says, "Understood."

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Hotline Worker
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The hotline guy says, yeah, call any time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so then the guy just hung up?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do we have any idea, like, whether he went through with it?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: No idea.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Were you able to find anybody who actually used the hotline, and then surrendered?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So I spent a lot of time trying to find someone who had done that, and I stumbled across an interview with a guy who tried. And he told his whole story.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So this is the guy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tell me about him.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He's young, 22 years old, kind of lanky. He was studying to be a computer programmer, and then was drafted into the army last fall.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because they have, like, mandatory military service in Russia, still.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. Every Russian guy has to do it. And there, he was assigned to be a rifleman and an assistant grenade launcher.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: But he had friends in Ukraine. And from the start of the invasion, he was very skeptical of the war.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And is he part of the invasion?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: No, at least not right away. But he says he has a close friend who was sent into combat and dies the first day of the war.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. And then, he starts talking to his other friend, the only person he really trusts, who's in the army with him. And they start talking about, maybe we should surrender. Like, maybe we should leave.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And at first, they're on the same page. But then, the closer they get to the front line, the less on-board his friend starts to get.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And one night, after he gets news of a successful counteroffensive in Kharkiv, he decides to go alone. He's actually in Russia. That's where he's based. And he says, after an eight-hour shift, he walks out of the barracks, heads west with a map and compass, and walks for two days.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This seems so dangerous. Like, the Ukrainians could see him coming and just decide to shoot him.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah. Or the Russians could see him fleeing. And after walking, finally, he makes it to the border.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And that's when he calls the hotline. The interviewer asks him about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, who is doing the interview?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So it's one of these two Ukrainian YouTubers who seem to have some connection with the Ukrainian government.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: The soldier says he heard about the hotline from friends living in Ukraine, and also, this girl, a good friend of his. The host asks, what's her name? She'll probably watch this.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He says, her name is Anya.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He reaches the hotline over Telegram. They told him to make his way to a village in Ukraine, where Ukrainian servicemen would be waiting for him. He got his last bits of energy together and started to make his way over.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: When I got to where they told me to go, it was sunset, not totally dark yet.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And I just looked at the village for a long time.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Truth be told, I was scared I wouldn't make it, that I'd just get shot. That was the scariest part.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And then, the interviewer interrupts. He says, seeing as you're here now, you didn't get shot. And he says, yeah, but I know what I look like in a Russian uniform. There could be an incident where I would get shot without any questions.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what happens.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: So once he gets there, he meets a Ukrainian woman and asks her for directions.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: She says, my kids can walk you there. They're going to come back alive, right? And he swears that he won't hurt anyone. So the kids walk him to the school gymnasium.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He gives the boy his pocketknife as a "thank you." And then, he's in--

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: How many times were you beaten?

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Not once.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: How about tortured?

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Never. In fact, they offered us candy and sweets. Though, I should point out, the UN has documented human rights abuses against Russian prisoners of war in Ukraine. They weren't reported to be systematic.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. Well, what about the fact that they're allowing video interviews with prisoners of war to go online?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yeah, that's potentially a violation of the Geneva Conventions. There are rules in there about not turning prisoners of war into subjects of public curiosity.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So then, after that, he's basically in a POW camp, like, waiting for a prisoner swap to go home?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I'm not sure he wants to go back. And I'm not sure what would happen to him if he did. He's given his full name on YouTube, admitting publicly he deserted the Russian army. Also, he says that he doesn't believe in Russia's version of the war. Like he says in the video, you're on your way to kill innocent people that are just defending their own country.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Then, when the interviewer asks him if he'd like to make a call home--

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He says, no, politely. His parents have different views on the war than him. Instead, he calls his friend, Anya, the one who told him about the hotline. There's a short clip of him on the phone.

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: He updates her on his status, and then says--

segments.speaker: Russian Soldier
segments.text: [RUSSIAN SPEECH]

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Tell me how you're doing. My life is such a mess right now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The way Russia sees the war and the way Ukraine sees it are like two different realities. But you know, there are so many places where that kind of thing is true, where one reality bumps up against another. And people try to coax each other across the line from one side to the other.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But crossing over-- not that many people do it, because it's so hard to do. It seems so dangerous. Today, on our program, we have people trying to sweet-talk each other across that line, with reason and with guile and with whatever they got. It's such an act of faith in each other even to try-- kind of inspiring, really. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us, please.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Flies, Meet Honey. So this woman, Aubree, has been calling elections administrators all over Texas for nearly two years. And as a case study of people trying to coax others over to their side, it's not going too well.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She questions them, accuses them. There's one call I want to play a little bit of-- kind of, sums things up. At the beginning of the call, the official is very calm, saying things like--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: Aubree, you brought up a lot of things, so I wanted to tackle them one by one.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But pretty quickly, Aubree is asking him about things that he can't comment on, because they're the subject of lawsuits. Lawyers have told them not to talk about them publicly. But Aubree-- she doesn't accept that. She keeps pushing.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: Your county attorneys-- they don't want you to give information to the voters?

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: All I'm telling you is, I'm following their advice, Aubree. And I look forward to a time when I'm able to talk more freely about this.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: So you're not able to talk freely about the issues in the elections, because one part of it has been filed with a court of law?

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: Aubree, did you not understand what I said earlier, when I said I'm not?

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: I do not. Could you help me understand--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: I think I've spoken clearly and in English that I have, that I can't speak about this, because of the current and ongoing litigation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As you can hear, this gets hotter and hotter. He's an elections administrator in a county in central Texas and has had years of Stop the Stealers now, questioning him like this. They flood elections offices with records requests. They sue.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Before long in this call, Aubree is quoting Texas legal code that she believes mandates that all ballots in Texas should be pre-numbered sequentially, starting at one, which isn't done today, with computers counting votes. And the elections administrator snaps.

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: What else would you like to quote, chapter and verse incorrectly?

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: OK, sure. Sure. So you're sitting in violation of the state and national constitutions, because the--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: Incorrect. Wrong. Next.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: Let me finish, sir. The Secretary of State does not have the authority to circumvent Texas election code, 52--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: You're mistaken. You're mistaken.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: No, I'm not.

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: I don't even have to let you finish. I can tell you right now, off the bat, you're mistaken. Next.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: Can you tell me the election code that you can cite, that allows you to circumvent the 52.062 and 62.009?

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: Request denied.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: You don't know it off the top of your head like I do? But you don't know the codes in the law off the top of your head?

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: I don't.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: OK. Do you-- have you read-- have you read the national--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: I'm pretty smart. Pretty smart. And yeah, I've read the Constitution.

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: It's not as [INAUDIBLE] that. But you're not. You're not. What you're going to-- no, here's what you're going to do.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: No, no, no, you're not going to tell me what I'm going to do. You're going to review-- you're going to review the national and state constitutions, is what's going to happen.

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: No, actually, it's not, Aubree--

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: Are you-- are you now refusing to review the national and state constitutions for your own--

segments.speaker: Official
segments.text: I am. And here's how I'm going to refuse that-- by the coming phone click that you're about to hear in 3, 2, 1.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because of these kinds of encounters between elections officials and activists, it gets very personal sometimes. In the last few years in Texas, lots of election administrators have quit or retired. The entire staff of an elections office in Gillespie County quit at the same time, because of accusations of fraud, obscene, racist emails, threats.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: People call the cops on these officials and try to get them arrested while they're doing their jobs. But there is another path. That woman, Aubree Campbell, that you just heard-- she happens to live in a county in Texas-- Tarrant County, where the elections administrator is not the guy who you just heard on the phone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The official in Tarrant County is this singular, kind of, remarkable figure. We learned about him from Natalia Contreras, who's been reporting on elections in Texas for months now, for Votebeat, which covers all this in depth around the country. Natalia says, there's really nobody else like him that she's been able to find.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He's very effective, for some special reasons that Natalia will explain in a bit. His name is Heider Garcia. And watching him, it's hard not to feel like if anybody could convince the election doubters that our elections can be trusted-- or at the very least, if anybody can make headway with them, it would be this guy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And to try to see how successful he is in winning over the election skeptics and the Stop the Stealers, and to see the limits of that success. Earlier this month, on election day, Natalia and Zoe Chace from our staff co-reported a story where the two of them followed Heider around as he managed the election in Tarrant County and as he dealt with the election doubters-- and Aubree, in particular. Here are Natalia and Zoe.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: Let's start with Aubree. She's just one of many people in Texas who have made it almost their full-time job to challenge election officials.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And they all have some kind of story like this to explain how they got into it. In Tarrant County, when Joe Biden won, it didn't really make any sense to Aubree. It's a Republican county. Republicans won down the ballot. But the president-- somehow, Biden won.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: Then, when Biden took Tarrant County, we were really upset, because Trump has a lot of vocal support here, and I don't know a single Democrat. And none of my Democrat friends voted for Biden in the primaries. They all voted for Bernie. So you talk to him one on one, they know something's not right.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: Aubree doesn't look like other activists I see in this world, who are mostly elderly and retired. She's 33, but looks way younger. She's white, petite, round, hipstery eyeglasses, leather jacket. She describes herself as a conservative metal head. She stands out.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: It was post-2020, because I remember the whole thing started with her interacting with an election judge.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: This is Heider Garcia.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: She was really frustrated. She took out her cell phone, started recording the poll worker, saying, you're obstructing me from voting. The poll worker said, you can't use your phone here, and the whole situation started to happen. And that's when I started interacting with her, and, you know.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: [RATTLING NOISE]

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: Coffee?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: It's 6:30 AM on election day. Heider Garcia is the kind of person who carries around his own coffee grinder to grind his own beans for his morning coffee. Fastidious? Neurotic? He has high standards for himself and his coffee.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He oversees every aspect of the election with the same fastidiousness. He sets the whole thing up. He trains the workers. He tells us he's been working on not being a micromanager, which you only say if you are.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: Heider's taking a particular approach with people like Aubree. It's something I haven't seen any other Texas election officials do. His strategy is to go as far as humanly possible to answer every question and address every suspicion. He treats everything they say like it's worthy of an answer.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: It's like radical patience. And when you see him do it, you see why other officials don't. Because it takes hours. It's a big part of his job now, on top of all the work of running an election.

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: They call with some issue. He's like, come in. Let me walk you through it. Let me show you around. Here's a typical example.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: So there was this one time when one of our watchers came in, and he was like, you know, if I-- he was in a tally room with us, and he said-- this was back in-- I think it was last year. If I were in charge here, I would make all the walls in this room glass, so that you could see where every cable goes, and you could be totally transparent-- something like that.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: And I looked at him and said, why do you want that? He says, well, because we should know where every wire goes, so we can know if you're connected to the internet or not. And I said, well, but the whole point is to show that the machines are not connected to the internet, right?

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: We're talking about the servers and the tally room, so there shouldn't be any cable going in the machine. So I told him, what about if we rearrange the room, so the machines are not, like, in this little cabinet under the desk, but up where you can see them and you can-- he said, well, maybe that would be a start.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: So the next election, they came back in a runoff. You know, when they walked in the room, I told them, all the machines are on top of the tables. You can see the back. They're against the glass.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: They're labeled what each one of them does. This is what you wanted, right? And so he had that moment of, again, OK, well, you got me on that one. And it's little things like that, that we keep doing, right?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: In theory, any election official could go this far-- answer every question-- if they wanted to. Though, in some ways, Heider's uniquely suited for this, he's a computer engineer. He's designed voting machines.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So he can answer, in detail, any question, technical or not, in a way few officials ever can. And for this election morning, as people are going out to vote, he's rigged up his office like some kind of air traffic control tower. It's a big room, and he's installed this enormous screen in it, and we're looking at every polling place marked on a huge Google map-- 316 of them.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: They're all color-coded with wait times. If there's a problem at a polling place, the color changes to mark the level of urgency-- low, medium, critical. Then, on a separate map, Heider can see, if a tech is dispatched to fix something, he can watch them travel out there on the map, like an Uber. We can see how long it's going to take. Not long after the polls open, around 8 AM, he gets a call.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: [KNOCKING ON DOOR]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Natalia Contreras
segments.text: Heider holds up the phone to me. He points at it and says, it's Aubree. Hey. Morning. Doing good.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell
segments.text: So there's a picture going around, and it's purported to be a map of outages of all of the machines. Is that-- are you having issues with that? This is, like, a lot. I'm going to send it to you to-- just so you see what this is.

segments.speaker: Heider Garcia
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Aubree Campbell

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Back in May, I became mildly obsessed with a stranger on TV. It was a big guy. He looked Black, biracial maybe, and he was wearing a light purple shirt under a black vest.

segments.text: A rideshare driver. I watch a lot of Jeopardy, but if you don't, you might not know that it is not that common among all the professors and the grad students and other learned contestants to see an Uber driver. Also unusual in my years of watching-- big Black guys.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Ryan won that first game, and then he kept on winning. In the end, he won almost $300,000 over 16 games, becoming the ninth winningest Jeopardy winner of all time. segments.text: Ryan, congratulations! With $18,800, you are our new Jeopardy champion.

segments.text: I took a photo of Ryan on my TV screen that first night he won, and posted it to Instagram. "You have my sword," I captioned the photo, a line from "The Lord of the Rings."

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Here's a thing about me-- I love trivia. I was a childhood library lurker who hoarded facts, just waiting to bust them out and impress people. I love remembering dates and locations, and I delight in wordplay.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Watching Ryan win again and again reminded me of myself a little, except he was me to the power of 100. It sounds condescending and weird, because we're about the same age, in our very late 30s, but I was proud of him, I think.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: I rarely feel affection for Jeopardy winners. They're too mannered, too serious, too odd. But I was rooting for Ryan. I felt like I knew him.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: He had tweeted after his winning run something that stuck with me, something about a box. "Sometimes," he wrote, "it seems like society put you in a box and you are classified as a certain thing, with a certain destiny, even though you may feel differently inside."

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: I wondered how somebody who felt so familiar to me had ended up dominating the Jeopardy stage. What was that like for him? What box did he think he was in, and how had Jeopardy helped him break out of it?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ryan, who's a big man now, describes himself as "husky" when he was a kid, which made him feel awkward and self-conscious. Plus, he was also in the midst of working out his mixed identity back then. His mom is Black and his father was white. And on top of that, he was an obviously smart kid. So they put him in the gifted classes, which also made him feel a little isolated.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I was smart and stupid at the same time. I had no idea how to relate to people. I lived in my head.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Uh-huh, which is good for accumulation of stuff, but--

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: --perhaps less useful--

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: But not great for relating to other people.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I used to downplay my intelligence like a motherfucker.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Like crazy. I would just stay quiet. Because I would have an opinion on a topic or something like that, and I was afraid that it would go over the other kids' heads and they would look at me like I got three eyes or something. So I would just keep my mouth shut. You feel like you got to fit in.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: This was his first understanding that people have ideas about you, and those ideas might not match how you feel about yourself. It was also the first time Ryan felt put into that box that he tweeted about. And in order to fit, he had to cut parts of himself off.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: In the end, Ryan didn't do great at school. His parents had split up when he was 13, and he'd gone to live with his dad. A few years later, when he was 17, his father died and Ryan moved back in with his mom.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: According to Ryan, he barely graduated high school, and then did a year of community college before dropping out. It's like he got so used to hiding away the brightest parts of himself, that he got really good at it-- too good. The way Ryan tells it, he settled into the role of underachiever, and that made him prone to self-sabotage.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: It'll be something like a subconscious thing where I know I got an important meeting or something, I got to be somewhere. And my brain, I'll have this urge to just, "you know what, just roll over."

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Instead of getting up because I know it's important, it's like, "Just roll over. Whatever. It doesn't mean that much. You don't need this. It's not that important. You don't want it."

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: And I'll oversleep, or I'll be late, or won't show up, something like that. It happens a lot, especially for things that could potentially benefit me. Because some part of me is either "this is stupid" or "you don't deserve it" or something. And I'm pretty sure that's depression.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: For all the potential of his big brain, Ryan had the feeling that life was slipping him by. And when he became a father in his 30s, the question of lost potential became moot. He needed money to live and to provide, so he did all sorts of jobs-- airport security worker, warehouse grunt, package handler, office clerk.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Piano mover, water ice guy, worked at UPS, was a cashier, was a bouncer, was a street sweeper for a couple of weeks. You got to do what you got to do, right?

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: But then in January 2021, Ryan got sick with COVID. He had it really bad, and was in hospital for three weeks. He had to be given oxygen to stay alive. And he still has the photo of his saturated lungs, given to him by his doctor as a reminder of how close he came to death.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: When he was discharged, he was a wreck. His knee gave out and he got diabetes. More than 20 years of the working grind seemed to catch up to him all at once.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I felt in the moment like I'd wasted my life thus far. I hadn't done anything I wanted to do. I hadn't gone anywhere that I wanted to go. I started feeling like maybe I didn't have a huge amount of time left.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: My dad died young. His dad died young. I didn't want to have to do that to my kid. I found my dad dead. I thought, if you're going to have a memory of me, have a good one.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Getting COVID and surviving it was, in Ryan's own words, "a rockfall that turned into a landslide." It made him want to get out of his old habit of minimizing himself, this urge to snatch defeats from the jaws of victory.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: That's when he got the call from Jeopardy. He'd taken the online test on a whim. And now, Ryan thought, this could be the thing he'd been hoping would come along to shake things up.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: That question I'd had about his journey to Jeopardy, it turns out the literal trip was a joint effort. He had about $200 to spare that month, and he had to make his own way to California. So he turned to his mom and his friends. He borrowed his mother's luggage and packed some black trousers plus two shirts-- one he'd bought himself, and the other bought by his mom.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Remember how he made the decision as a teenager to hide his light under a bushel so he could be more normal? Now he was making another decision-- this time the guy whose tendency was to downplay his intelligence and his abilities was not going to get in his own way.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: The work was on me where I had to first acknowledge that I wanted it, give myself permission to want it. And say, OK, we're going to do this thing and we're going to do it right and we're not going to screw it up.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: He got on the plane to California. He'd never been off the east coast in his life. He was determined to enjoy himself. And he told himself, no expectations. Unlike some other wannabe winners, he did no tutorials on technique, no arduous studying.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: These are people that all year long they study, buying books on the buzzer technique and all that. When I've found out that people did that, [LAUGHS] I felt like, oh, should I have studied? I guess, maybe.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: You didn't pick up "The Big Book of Jeopardy Questions?"

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I didn't have time. I was working. I was working up until right before I left.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: On the day of his first game Ryan felt overwhelmed, but he worked through it. He let himself cry, which was an effective release valve for some of the emotional turmoil he was feeling. And then he pumped himself up with some music. Once he felt more in control, he headed to the studio to the show he'd watched since he was a little boy in Philly.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Felt like hallowed ground-- Jeopardy, the stage. When you get up there, it looks exactly like when Luke fought Vader on Bespin in "The Empire Strikes Back," the lighting.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: The red stair and then the blue background, that was the first thing I noticed when I got up there. I was like, oh, my god! Really felt like something, man.

segments.speaker: Mayim Bialik
segments.text: --Sawyer and Tyrion Lannister. Ryan?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Who is Peter Dinklage?

segments.speaker: Mayim Bialik
segments.text: Yes, and you just ran that category.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: So that was a somewhat nerdy beginning of his 16-game streak. He puts the success down to two things-- knowing stuff and staying calm under pressure.

segments.speaker: Mayim Bialik
segments.text: Ryan?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Who was Jesse Owens?

segments.speaker: Mayim Bialik
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: In game mode, Ryan's demeanor was testament to the decision he'd made to go out there and just have fun. He laughed at himself when he flubbed the Daily Double, or realized he had bet too low on an easy answer. He delivered his cute little anecdotes in the "getting to know you" segments. But once the game was won, that easy grace was gone.

segments.speaker: Mayim Bialik
segments.text: Congratulations, you are our Jeopardy champion. Another fantastic week for Ryan Long.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Instead, when his new total winnings were announced, he'd do that thing I loved. The head duck, and looking like he wanted the ground to swallow him up.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I couldn't believe it I heard it every time.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Every time?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Every time I heard it, I was like, this-- nah. I don't think I could-- that didn't happen to me, [LAUGHS] you know?

segments.speaker: Brad Pearson
segments.text: So I guess Ryan and I met on the very first day. Well, my only day of taping on Jeopardy, and Ryan's second day, I guess it was?

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: That's Brad Pearson. He was a challenger of Ryan's, also a Philly local. The two of them stayed friends after the show. They even had a little watch party at Brad's house the night his episode aired.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Over cheesesteaks, he told us about playing against Ryan in his fifth game. Contestants get to watch preceding games before they tape theirs. And all eyes were on Ryan, the returning champ, game after game. Brad was sitting with Tony, another of the pool of challengers.

segments.speaker: Brad Pearson
segments.text: As the day progressed, Tony turns to me at one point during the third game, and he goes, "He's only getting stronger!"

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Brad noted the same thing I did-- that Ryan was a real all-rounder, banging out answers to everything from biblical locations, to the alumni of Saturday Night Live.

segments.speaker: Brad Pearson
segments.text: When I think of Ryan as a player, the thing is that you find certain people that are good at some really specific stuff. But Ryan's knowledge is so across the board, and also does really good on things that--

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I got to go take a walk.

segments.speaker: Brad Pearson
segments.text: This is going to sound bad, but--

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Ryan actually moved away when Brad was talking about him so admiringly. It's like the glare of praise was too bright for his eyes. He couldn't look directly at it. He did something similar when his mom bragged about him, and again when his friend Mari, who we also met, mentioned how great of a guy he was.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: His face got all scrunched up, like it physically pained him to hear. But even so, over the course of his games, he beat contestants with far more impressive on-paper CVs. Even after winning, he knew that he wasn't seen as a typical Jeopardy winner.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I don't look smart, whatever that means. I look like a bruiser.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: And people underestimate me a lot. I know I'm kind of smart. I know what I can do. There was a little tiny bit of class satisfaction. I don't mind admitting it--

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: --that I came in and beat all these wonderful people. People like my mom, people like me, we've always watched the show. We've just never been represented on the show before, I guess you could say. But we're out here.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Ryan's tweet thread about the box, he'd written that he didn't really believe a person could break out of the box. But, he added, I feel like this thing that just happened is proof that you can. And I wondered what he'd found outside of the box since he had managed to get out.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Returning to Philly, it was hard for Ryan to know how to act. His episodes wouldn't be on television for another few weeks. It was like he had to pretend something monumental hadn't just happened to him.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: There's no way to talk about Ryan's time on the show without talking about the money he won. $299,400 is quite the windfall. He no longer works as a rideshare driver, having paid off his old car and bought this new truck.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: On the advice of his mom, he met up with a couple of people from a community improvement group for advice about what to do with this new earnings. Their advice was that he prioritize himself first, a concept that was completely foreign to him, and set up a chain reaction of self improvements.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I wasn't a very reflective person, or anything like that, and I neglected myself for about 30 years. So I figured now is the time. I have a rare chance, which it seems like a lot of Americans don't have anymore. Because I got time to improve myself, take a real good look at myself, you know?

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Ryan started working out again. He got himself a therapist. He went digging in his family tree and found a book written by his third-time great grandfather, a staunch Methodist abolitionist. And he bought movies.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: I love, love, love films. I'll buy the extra special deluxe, whatever, whatever, if I can. So every July, The Criterion sale is 50% off, and every year something happens and I can't afford to go. And I was like, I'm going this year. [SNAPS] Going!

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: [LAUGHS] What's the first one you're going to watch, do you reckon?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Oh, you know, I think I'm going to watch Raging Bull. I heard The Criterion was coming out with the 4K, I was like, oh, my god, yes! It's so great. It's a great movie-- difficult to watch though.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Horrible to watch--

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: --in places.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Difficult, but it's also difficult because every man can recognize a part of himself in Jake LaMotta-- like some small part, some of us more than others. But we all have that ugly competitive sort of thing inside us, however small, or that ugly, self-loathing type beast.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Getting to finally buy Criterion movies, working on his LaMotta style self-loathing, spending hours researching family history, the whole "Project Ryan," it's being facilitated by the most precious commodity his Jeopardy run brought him.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: So, clearly, Jeopardy changed your life. So what is your life now?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: It allowed me the opportunity to have time to do this, which I wouldn't have had time to do anyway.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: What's this?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: It-- examine myself, I guess. Just everything before, looking where I come from and what makes me tick. It's a valuable thing. I think everybody needs to do it, but not everybody has time to do it.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: So that's the biggest post-Jeopardy change is just an abundance of time for you now?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Yeah. That's the most valuable thing that I got out of this.

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: Not the money?

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: Well, the money made the time possible. They say money can't buy happiness, but it buys everything that makes you happy-- even time.

segments.speaker: Ryan Long
segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]

segments.speaker: Bim Adewunmi
segments.text: I had come to Philly to talk to Ryan about navigating outside expectations as they crashed up against what he thought about himself, and I got that. But I also got this accidental reflection on American capitalism, and how so many of us are served so poorly by the way life is currently set up as all work and no time. Jeopardy provided a very specific Ryan-shaped escape hatch. It gave him the space to stare into that crack between realities, and fish out all the elements of what his life could be.

segments.speaker: Torey Malatia
segments.text: Three, two, one?
